bull.b: Entergy's regulated utility model produces durable margins (TTM net margin ~13.6%, EBITDA ~44.5%), indicating steady earnings power under rate-recovery mechanisms. Strong margins support ongoing returns on invested capital and provide resilience through demand cycles and regulatory ratemaking.

Operating cash flow has improved materially to roughly $6.1B TTM from ~$5.2B, creating a more reliable internal funding source. Higher OCF reduces near-term refinancing pressure, helps sustain credit metrics, and partially offsets heavy capex needs while supporting regulated capital recovery over multiple years.

The $57B four-year plan and the Meta agreement (fair-share ~$2B) provide multi-year load visibility and rate-base growth. Signed ESAs and a 7–12 GW data-center pipeline translate into predictable, customer-backed investment that should support sustainable long-term revenue and EPS growth as assets are placed in service.

bear.b: Entergy's debt-to-equity near 1.96 reflects meaningfully elevated leverage for a utility. High leverage reduces financial flexibility, raises refinancing sensitivity to rate moves, and constrains the company's ability to absorb cost overruns or pursue opportunistic investments without additional external financing.

Despite improving OCF, Entergy's FCF remains about -$3.1B TTM as required capex outstrips internal cash generation. Persistent negative FCF increases dependence on capital markets, limits organic funding for dividends or share buybacks, and makes long-term capital programs contingent on continued financing access.

bear.t: Financing & execution risk from big capex
bear.b: Management plans $6.6B of equity for the four-year plan but has only contracted ~$1.9B, leaving ~$4.7B to raise later. Combined with use of forward sales/offerings, this reliance on equity and external funding creates dilution risk and execution/timing risk when delivering large transmission, CCCTs and storage projects.
